metadata.description: Phase 9: Logic drift report - every transformation logic difference, which version was adopted, and why

drift_findings.description: Each platform ranks Paid, Adjusted, Denied, and Reversed claims in a different priority order during dedup. Different orders produce different output claim counts and financial totals.

teradata_implementation.assessment: INCORRECT - Prefers DENIED over ADJUSTED, which causes valid adjusted claims to be dropped in favor of denied claims. This inflates denial rates and understates paid amounts.

databricks_implementation.assessment: CORRECT - Follows CMS standard priority ordering. PAID claims take highest priority, then adjustments (which represent the most current billing state), then denials, then reversals.

snowflake_implementation.assessment: PARTIALLY INCORRECT - Swaps REVERSED and DENIED. Prefers reversed claims over denied claims, which could retain reversed (voided) claims when a denial exists.

drift_findings.rationale: CMS Pub 100-04 Chapter 1 Section 80.3.2 defines the standard claim adjustment hierarchy: Original > Adjusted > Denied > Reversed. The Databricks implementation correctly follows this standard.
drift_findings.business_impact: Teradata ADR bug caused ~3-5% overcounting of denied claims and ~2% undercounting of paid amounts in financial reports. Snowflake REVERSED/DENIED swap had minimal impact since both are non-paid statuses.

drift_findings.description: Teradata uses naive GROUP BY for encounter grouping, while Databricks and Snowflake use gap-and-island overlap detection. Naive grouping does not correctly merge overlapping service date ranges.

teradata_implementation.algorithm: Naive GROUP BY member_id, service_date_from, service_date_to
teradata_implementation.assessment: INCORRECT - Only groups claims with exact matching dates. Two claims for the same member with dates [Jan 1 - Jan 5] and [Jan 3 - Jan 8] would be counted as separate encounters instead of one merged encounter.

databricks_implementation.algorithm: Gap-and-island with LAG window function detecting date range overlaps
databricks_implementation.assessment: CORRECT - Properly detects overlapping date ranges and merges them into single encounters.

snowflake_implementation.algorithm: Gap-and-island with running MAX(end_date) window function
snowflake_implementation.assessment: CORRECT - Same algorithm as Databricks, different SQL syntax.

drift_findings.rationale: AHRQ HCUP definition of an encounter requires merging overlapping service dates. Naive GROUP BY violates this standard and inflates encounter counts.
drift_findings.business_impact: Teradata naive grouping inflated encounter counts by ~15-25% for inpatient claims with multi-day stays. This overstated utilization metrics and biased PMPM calculations upward.

drift_findings.description: Each platform stores diagnosis codes in a fundamentally different structure, affecting how downstream joins and queries work.

teradata_implementation.structure: 25 individual VARCHAR(10) columns: icd_diagnosis_code_1 through icd_diagnosis_code_25
teradata_implementation.assessment: Widely compatible but verbose. Requires UNION ALL for flattening.

databricks_implementation.assessment: Modern and flexible but requires explode() for row-level analysis.

snowflake_implementation.structure: Hybrid: VARIANT JSON array (diagnosis_codes_json) + 10 individual VARCHAR columns
snowflake_implementation.assessment: Redundant storage but provides both access patterns.

drift_findings.rationale: Tuva input layer expects individual diagnosis code columns (diagnosis_code_1..25). This is the CMS 837/UB-04 standard format (up to 25 diagnosis codes per claim).
drift_findings.business_impact: No analytical impact - all three approaches contain the same data, just structured differently. Performance impact: individual columns are more efficient for specific diagnosis code lookups, arrays are better for 'any diagnosis' searches.

drift_findings.description: PHI (Protected Health Information) masking is applied at different stages in each platform's pipeline, creating compliance risk.

teradata_implementation.strategy: Post-mart masking via stored procedure (sp_phi_masking). Masking applied AFTER mart layer creation.
teradata_implementation.assessment: HIPAA RISK - Raw PHI is accessible in staging and intermediate tables. Any analyst with access to these tables can see unmasked PHI.

databricks_implementation.strategy: ETL-time masking at staging layer. PySpark notebook applies SHA-256 hash during ingestion.
databricks_implementation.assessment: Secure but IRREVERSIBLE - PHI is permanently hashed at ingestion. Cannot be unmasked even by authorized users who need original values.

snowflake_implementation.strategy: Dynamic Data Masking policies on columns. Masking applied at query time based on user role.
snowflake_implementation.assessment: BEST APPROACH - Role-based, reversible, applied at query time. Authorized roles see original data, unauthorized roles see masked values.

drift_findings.rationale: HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(a)(1) requires access controls for PHI. Dynamic masking provides role-based access control without destroying data fidelity. OCR guidance supports query-time masking as a valid technical safeguard.
drift_findings.business_impact: Teradata approach had HIPAA audit findings risk. Databricks approach prevented clinical data analysis requiring original values. Snowflake approach balances security with utility.
drift_findings.unified_implementation: Snowflake Dynamic Data Masking policies preserved on RAW tables. dbt models inherit masking from source.

drift_findings.description: When deduplicating member records, platforms use different tiebreaking sort orders.

teradata_implementation.sort_order: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY load_date DESC)
teradata_implementation.assessment: Sorts by load_date only. If two records have the same load_date, the result is non-deterministic.

databricks_implementation.sort_order: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY coverage_start_date DESC, _load_timestamp DESC)
databricks_implementation.assessment: Sorts by coverage_start_date then load_timestamp. More deterministic.

snowflake_implementation.sort_order: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY eligibility_start_date DESC, source_load_timestamp DESC)

drift_findings.rationale: Using enrollment_start_date as the primary sort ensures the most recent enrollment record is retained. Adding source_load_timestamp as tiebreaker ensures deterministic results.
drift_findings.business_impact: Minimal. Teradata's non-deterministic sort could cause inconsistent member counts across runs when records share the same load_date.

drift_findings.description: Databricks uses DOUBLE (floating point) for financial amounts while Teradata and Snowflake use fixed-precision DECIMAL/NUMBER.

teradata_implementation.assessment: Correct for financial data. Fixed precision prevents rounding errors.

databricks_implementation.assessment: INCORRECT for financial data. IEEE 754 floating point can introduce rounding errors (e.g., 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3).

drift_findings.rationale: Financial calculations require fixed-precision arithmetic. IEEE 754 DOUBLE can produce rounding errors that accumulate across millions of claims. Industry standard is DECIMAL/NUMBER for monetary values.
drift_findings.business_impact: Databricks DOUBLE could produce rounding discrepancies of ~$0.01 per claim, accumulating to thousands of dollars in aggregate reports. Financial audits could flag these discrepancies.
drift_findings.unified_implementation: All staging models cast financial columns to NUMBER(18,2)

drift_findings.description: Platforms use different string encodings for the same claim types.

teradata_implementation.assessment: Single-character codes. 'O' for Outpatient is non-standard (should be mapped to Professional for facility claims).

databricks_implementation.assessment: Full text values. OUTPATIENT is a subcategory of either Institutional or Professional.

snowflake_implementation.assessment: Two values only. No Outpatient distinction.

drift_findings.rationale: Tuva input layer uses two claim types matching CMS standard: institutional (facility) and professional. Outpatient is a place of service, not a claim type.
drift_findings.business_impact: Teradata 'O' claims need manual review to determine correct mapping. In most cases, Outpatient facility claims are 'institutional' and Outpatient professional claims are 'professional'.
drift_findings.unified_implementation: CASE statements in all staging models normalize claim types

summary.primary_source_of_truth: Databricks had the most correct implementations (5 of 7 adopted from Databricks or Databricks+Snowflake). Snowflake had the best PHI masking approach. Teradata had no implementations adopted as-is.
